children: OTTAWA--Canada's industry minister on Wednesday opened the door to financial incentives for Stellantis to keep a Toronto-area factory open for motor-vehicle production.

Melanie Joly said the federal government stands ready to do what is feasible to maintain auto production at Stellantis's Brampton, Ontario, factory, and persuade the automaker to call off a tentative sale of the plant to a Canadian producer of armored cars.

Amid hefty Trump administration tariffs on foreign-made cars, Stellantis decided last year to shift planned production of its Jeep Compass model to Illinois from Brampton. The company said it would pursue a sale of the factory because of a weak financial case to continue production--a move that puts over 2,000 jobs at risk.

"When it comes to Stellantis, we're dealing with the impacts of American tariffs," said Joly, prior to a weekly meeting of members of the governing Liberal Party. She said the Canadian government is willing to play a role in helping Stellantis, like Ottawa did in providing financial help to Ford and Honda.
This marks a subtle change of tone from Joly, who has repeatedly threatened to file a lawsuit against Stellantis to recoup money it provided the company to retool its Canadian plants.

Joly said she spoke with a Stellantis executive Tuesday night, and representatives for the automaker, federal and regional governments, and organized labor are in Toronto discussing the future of the Brampton plant.

A spokeswoman for Stellantis said the company's focus in these talks is the future of its Canadian operations and its roughly 9,000 employees. A spokeswoman for Unifor, the union that represents Canadian autoworkers, said the parties have agreed to hold further talks, but provided no further details.

Last week, Canada unveiled a finalized pact to provide about $300 million to Ford after the company began production on heavy-duty pickup trucks, following a plant retooling that began before President Trump imposed auto tariffs.
Trade-policy experts told Canadian senators Wednesday that offering additional financial incentives to Stellantis and other automakers is unwise policy.

"I think the political challenge is to level with Canadians and to stop pretending that by throwing money at the [auto] sector we can keep it alive," said Fen Hampson, professor of international affairs at Ottawa's Carleton University. "I think the challenge is how to do you begin to redeploy capital and labor in a way that those who are losing their jobs will find new jobs."
Data analyzed by London-based ISI Markets indicate auto production in Canada has dropped sharply, by nearly 60%, since hitting a peak in 1999.
